extracted_by: hand, T-0292 — the Democrat read, October 1834
note: Vol. I No. 44, the first issue of the month, and the one that PRINTS THE ORDINANCES FIRST — the four wards and their fire wardens, the stove-pipe code with the three-inch clearance the later witness loses, and the ordinance of 29 September forbidding anyone to carry earth off a Chicago street. Its transcription is the poorest of the five: page 3 column 1 is destroyed down its left edge and the advertising columns are half-crops, so most of this issue's advertisements are read here only where they add something their cleaner reprints later in the month do not carry — E. Rider's two-storey store and dwelling next door to the Post Office and nearly opposite the drawbridge, and Pierce & French's forge on the corner of Lake street opposite the Chicago Hotel. No post-office list: the 1 October list first appears a week later.

claims.notes: THE FIRST PRINTING OF THE ORDINANCE THAT DIVIDED CHICAGO INTO FOUR WARDS, one week ahead of the cleaner reading at 1834-10-08 page 4 column 4 (claim c001 there). Both are kept because each closes gaps in the other: this witness carries the DATE OF THE MEETING — the 20th day of September 1834 — which the later printing loses, and the later one carries the second ward's closing street, EAST Water, which this one loses. Read together they give the boundaries whole: first ward east of the centre of Lasalle between Jackson and South Water; second west of Lasalle between Jackson and East Water; third north of the river; fourth west of the branches. THE COLUMN IS DESTROYED DOWN ITS LEFT EDGE — every line loses its first eight to twelve characters to the neighbouring column — so the supplies here are the heaviest in the October run, and every one of them is either a word closed from its own sentence or a phrase printed whole in the 1834-10-08 witness. The word read `fine ssparate` is supplied `four` because four wards and no more are then enumerated in the same sentence. Nothing is supplied that neither witness carries. THE WARDENS ARE RECORDED AT THE STRENGTH THE TWO PRINTINGS SUPPORT AND NO FURTHER: `Edward Hunter` carries no middle initial, because this witness reads `F.` and the other carries none; the third warden is `Resigue` by surname only, because this witness reads his forename `Sumnel` and the other reads it `Eepael`.

claims.notes: THE CLEARANCE THE OTHER WITNESS LOSES. 1834-10-08's printing of this same section cuts out at 'shall the pipe of any stove be nea[rer than …] inches', and here the number survives: THREE INCHES from a stove or its pipe to any woodwork. That is a dimension a reconstruction can build to, and it is the only one either witness gives. Everything else agrees with the fuller reading — pipes out through the ROOF and never through a side or an end; a stone or earthenware cylinder, a brick surround, or a tin or sheet-iron plate held a quarter of an inch clear; and houses whose partitions are wood or lath and plaster. The distance a pipe must stand proud of the roof is cut in both printings and stays a gap in both.

claims.notes: THE STREETS OF CHICAGO WERE MADE OF SOMETHING WORTH STEALING. Nine days after drawing its wards the same board forbade anyone to carry EARTH away from a street inside the corporation except by the supervisor of roads' order and to repair the street with. Two things for a reconstruction. The 1834 street surface is EARTH — loose, cartable, and maintained by moving more of it about. And the town has a SUPERVISOR OF ROADS, an office this corpus meets here for the first time; the July 1834 run had the Surveyor graduating South Water Street to a crown (1834-07-30, claim c001) and this is the officer who afterwards keeps it. Both readings of this ordinance are damaged — the second is at 1834-10-08 page 4 column 4 (claim c004 there) — and between them the fine and the commencement date are still partly cut, so both are left bracketed. The meeting is again at the TREMONT HOUSE, which is where the board sat all autumn.

claims.notes: A BUILDING PLACED THREE WAYS AT ONCE, and every one of them useful. TWO STOREYS, framed, built to be a store below and a dwelling above; ON SOUTH WATER STREET; NEARLY OPPOSITE THE DRAWBRIDGE; and NEXT DOOR TO THE POST OFFICE. The drawbridge is the crossing of the main stem and the post office is J. S. C. Hogan's, whose store and whose lot this month's other columns name twice more (1834-10-08 claim c009, 1834-10-29 claim c003) — so this advertisement ties the post office to a South Water Street frontage near the bridge, which is a placement for the post office as much as for the building for sale. It also corroborates the stove and tin dealer's 'store in Water-st., near the bridge' in the same week (1834-10-08, claim c008): that stretch of South Water by the drawbridge is where the paper says the best stands for business are. THE COLUMN IS A HALF-CROP and the advertisement survives as broken clauses; the word before 'Building' is lost and 'frame' is supplied only because a two-storey building suitable for a store and dwelling in 1834 Chicago is a frame one — that is an INFERENCE and it is bracketed and stated here as one.

claims.notes: THE TAILOR WHO HAD NO SHOP, AND THE THREE HOUSES THAT VOUCHED FOR HIM. Thomas S. Eels takes orders at G. S. Hubbard & Co.'s store rather than at premises of his own, and gives Hubbard & Co., Newberry & Dole and John H. Kinzie as references — the three biggest commercial names in the paper, printed as a list of who would speak for a tradesman in 1834. That is a documented shape of business: a skilled man working out of a merchant's counter, with no frontage to letter. By 22 October a firm called ANDREWS & EELLS has 'commenced the Tailoring business' with premises of its own at the Tremont House (1834-10-22, claim c011); the surname is the same and the succession is obvious, but the corpus does not merge names on obviousness and no `identity.json` rule is declared. This printing is cut into fragments; a cleaner one stands at 1834-10-08 page 3 column 3 and is what the supplies above are read from.

claims.notes: A SECOND FORGE, AT A CORNER, WITH A PREDECESSOR FIRM NAMED. Two things here that a reconstruction can use and one that it must not overread. The corner is on LAKE STREET and the cross street is lost — a `corner` placement whose anchor is therefore recorded as 'Lake street, opposite the Chicago Hotel' rather than as a crossing, because naming the second street would be inventing it. The CHICAGO HOTEL is a new landmark for this corpus, and October 1834's advertising leans on five named houses in all — the Tremont House, the Eagle Hotel, Haddock's Tavern, the Exchange Coffee House and this one. And 'Pierce and Abbott' is a SUCCESSION: the same stand, an earlier partnership. The column is a half-crop and this advertisement survives as scattered clauses, so the supplies are heavy, every one is bracketed, and the trade — blacksmith work — is the one thing the heading states outright.

claims.notes: A WATER LOT, NUMBERED, IN KINZIE'S ADDITION. This is a plat reference of the kind the October run gives only twice — the other is Lot 7 in Block 16 on Lake Street (1834-10-15, claim c005) — and it is the only one that names a WATER lot, which is to say a parcel with river frontage on the north bank. The vendor's line is cut here and is printed whole in 1834-10-29 page 3 column 2 (`ATE Lot No. 12, in Kinzio's Addition, and Lots 2, 7 and 8, in block 5. Sept. 10, H. PEARSONS.`), which is where the block number and the seller are read from; both are bracketed here. H. Pearsons is also the man forbidding timber-cutting and trespass on the north-east quarter of section 4 in a township and range the notice names but this run has not resolved to ground (1834-10-15 page 3 column 2), so he is a landholder rather than a storekeeper.

claims.notes: CHICAGO ADVERTISING ITSELF AS A WHOLESALE PLACE, IN 1834. The pitch is aimed at 'dealers in the interior' and its argument is explicit: buy here rather than going to ST. LOUIS OR THE EAST, because these goods came straight from New York importers. That is the town claiming to be a distribution point for the country behind it a year before the scene date, and it is the clearest statement of Chicago's commercial role anywhere in this month's paper. The same notice runs in 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2 in a cleaner state, which is what the supplies here are read from.

claims.notes: THE SCHOOL SECTION IS BEING SOLD OFF BY THE CANAL COMMISSIONERS' PLAT, and the men selling it are the county's own officers — Richard J. Hamilton, who signs this month's tax list as Clerk of the Commissioners' Court (1834-10-29, claim c005) and elsewhere as Commissioner of School Lands for Cook County (1834-10-08 page 3 column 3). For a reconstruction the useful fact is the LAYOUT AUTHORITY: the ground immediately west and south of the original plat was surveyed by the Illinois and Michigan Canal commissioners, so its block and lot numbering is theirs and not the 1830 town plat's. G. Blanshard is selling on the same section in the same month (1834-10-22, claim c004). The reading is a half-crop and the cleaner printing at 1834-10-15 page 3 column 2 supplies the bracketed clauses.
